column4: The section defines رَبَّاهُ under root ر ب ب as raising a child through stages, and makes the orphan's reaching maturity the endpoint. This ayah names two orphan boys, protects their property, and says their Lord intended them to reach full strength (يَبْلُغَا أَشُدَّهُمَا); it makes the same care concrete as protection over time.

The section's child is taken into a household and entrusted to a caretaker. Moses' sister offers “أَهْلِ بَيْتٍ يَكْفُلُونَهُ لَكُمْ” (a household to care for him), showing how a vulnerable child can be placed with a family while his mother is absent.

The section's sheltering of a fatherless child is joined here to safe reunion: God returns the infant to his mother so that she may be comforted and not grieve. This completes the care arrangement proposed in 28:12.

The section's dictionary branch under root ر ب ب says a man “raised his child”; Pharaoh uses the same raising sense in “أَلَمْ نُرَبِّكَ فِينَا وَلِيدًا” (“Did we not raise you among us as a child?”). The question turns upbringing into a claim of debt; 26:22 supplies Moses' answer and exposes the coercive setting.

Moses calls the alleged favor “وَتِلْكَ نِعْمَةٌ تَمُنُّهَا عَلَيَّ” and identifies Israel's enslavement as its substance. This completes 26:18's reminder of being raised in Pharaoh's house, marking the boundary between care that protects a child and power that uses care as leverage.

The section defines upbringing as carrying a child through stages toward completion. In Moses' infancy, God says “وَلِتُصْنَعَ عَلَىٰ عَيْنِي” (that you be brought up under My care), placing the child’s protection and upbringing under a watchful guardian.

This retelling of Moses' rescue says his sister offers to identify someone who will care for him, then he is returned to his mother so she may be comforted and not grieve. It repeats the section's scene of a vulnerable child placed in care and protected through reunion.

Pharaoh's wife asks that the infant be spared and says he may become “قُرَّتُ عَيْنٍ لِي وَلَكَ” or be taken as a son. The section's home receives a vulnerable child; this scene makes the household's decision to welcome and protect a child explicit.

The section presents being taken into a home as refuge. Here Pharaoh's household takes in Moses, yet the verse calls him a future enemy and grief to them; it is a specific reversal showing that a household can receive a child without becoming a merciful shelter.

The section centers on a vulnerable child whose safety depends on another's care. This ayah shows Moses' mother nursing him and placing him in the river under God's instruction; 28:8 completes the sequence when Pharaoh's household picks him up. This ayah's own contribution is the mother's protective act during separation.

The section describes a person who takes responsibility for a child and the provision available within a home. This ayah says “وَكَفَّلَهَا زَكَرِيَّا” and that Zakariya found provision with Mary, showing a guardian's care joined to material sustenance.

The section names the one who attends to a child as a caretaker. This ayah recounts the people casting lots over who would assume Mary's care (“أَيُّهُمْ يَكْفُلُ مَرْيَمَ”), a direct scene of assigning guardianship.

The section names الرَّابّ under root ر ب ب as the person who takes charge of a stepchild, and الرَّبِيبَة as the woman who nurtures a child. The verse uses “وَرَبَائِبُكُمُ اللَّاتِي فِي حُجُورِكُمْ” for stepdaughters in a man's care, making the household's fostering relation explicit.

The section defines the orphan as a child whose father died before maturity. This ayah tests orphans until they reach marriageable age and sound judgment, then orders their property returned; its endpoint closely matches the section's age boundary.

The section describes a child being received into a household. In answering about orphans, this ayah permits living with them and calls them “فَإِخْوَانُكُمْ” (your brothers), framing care as shared family life rather than distance.

The section develops a household enlarged by marriage and the care of children. This ayah specifically names orphan women whose prescribed rights are withheld while men desire to marry them; it exposes the household's power to exploit the person it should shelter and makes justice a condition of marriage.

The section says marriage enlarges a household. This ayah makes marriage with orphan girls conditional on fearing injustice to them, and directs men who fear that injustice to marry other women; it draws a boundary around taking an orphan into a marital household.

The section's guardian is responsible for a child in the home. This ayah orders guardians to give orphans their property and forbids consuming it into their own, spelling out a material duty that protects the dependent from the household's power.

The section's home is meant to sustain a child. This ayah says those who consume orphan property unjustly consume fire into their bellies, a direct reversal of the provider's duty to protect and maintain the orphan.

The section places the orphan's vulnerability before his reaching maturity. This ayah forbids approaching an orphan's property except in the best manner until he reaches maturity, making the guardian's restraint last through the child's dependence.

The section defines yatim as fatherless until maturity and then turns to how the orphan should be treated. This ayah protects the orphan's property “حَتَّىٰ يَبْلُغَ أَشُدَّهُ” and supplies the same endpoint for that protection.

When relatives, orphans, and the needy are present at an inheritance division, this ayah says to give them provision from it and speak kindly. It puts the dependent and orphan inside the family distribution scene developed by the section.

The section's home takes in a needy child; this ayah describes feeding an orphan, a needy person, and a captive out of love for God. It makes provision for the vulnerable a chosen act rather than a claim on them.
The section identifies the orphan by the loss of a father. This ayah names an orphan who is close of kin and must be fed in a day of hunger, joining kinship, need, and concrete support.
The section turns from being sheltered to the command not to humiliate an orphan. This ayah rebukes people who do not honor the orphan, a direct social reversal of the home that receives the child.
The section ends by forbidding the humiliation of an orphan. This ayah depicts the contrary act, one who “يَدُعُّ الْيَتِيمَ” (shoves the orphan away), making the denied shelter visible as rejection.

The section's dictionary form آوى under root ء و ي means taking another into one's home. This ayah recalls a small, weakened community and says God gave them refuge, support, and provision (“فَآوَاكُمْ وَأَيَّدَكُم بِنَصْرِهِ وَرَزَقَكُم”); it expands household shelter into communal protection.

The section's dictionary form آوى describes sheltering another. This ayah names believers who migrated and those who gave refuge and help (“آوَوا وَّنَصَرُوا”), presenting shelter as a reciprocal community duty.

This ayah repeats the section's sheltering scene with believers who “آوَوا وَّنَصَرُوا,” then connects that support to forgiveness and provision. It shows the receiving household as part of a wider practice of refuge.

The section's dictionary form آوى means to shelter someone. This ayah says God sheltered Mary and her son on a secure height with flowing water (“وَآوَيْنَاهُمَا إِلَىٰ رَبْوَةٍ ذَاتِ قَرَارٍ وَمَعِينٍ”), pairing protection with a place to live and sustenance.

The section's dictionary form آوى names taking refuge. This ayah says the young men sought refuge in the cave and asked for mercy and right direction, a scene of vulnerable youths turning to shelter when their surroundings fail them.

The young men in 18:10 seek refuge from their people; this ayah completes that scene with their companion's instruction to take refuge in the cave (“فَأْوُوا إِلَى الْكَهْفِ”). Its own contribution is the practical act of finding a protected place.

The section's dictionary form آوى means taking someone into one's shelter. When Joseph's brothers arrive, he takes his brother Benjamin close to himself (“آوَىٰ إِلَيْهِ أَخَاهُ”), making shelter an intimate act within a separated family.

The section's household is a place people return to and are received. Joseph takes his parents to himself (“آوَىٰ إِلَيْهِ أَبَوَيْهِ”) and welcomes them into Egypt; this portrays a grown child making a secure home for his family.

The section's dictionary account of آل describes a household whose return is to one another. After the family enters in 12:99, this ayah shows Joseph's parents and family reunited around him, completing the return of kin to a household.

The section describes a household that receives and provides for someone in need. This ayah praises the people who settled in the home before the emigrants, loved those who came to them, and preferred them over themselves even when needy; it is a direct host-and-refuge community.

The section's child is sheltered after loss and vulnerability. This ayah promises those who migrated after being wronged that God will settle them in a good place, carrying the image of refuge into a new home after persecution.

The section makes home a place of shelter. This ayah describes leaving one's home in migration and finding on earth “مُرَاغَمًا كَثِيرًا وَسَعَةً” (room and spaciousness), a specific promise that displacement can open into refuge.
This ayah says God made houses for people as places of rest (“سَكَنًا”), giving a direct account of what the section's receiving home provides: settled shelter for those who live in it.

The section's dictionary account of آل describes a household as a place of mutual return, while its central scene gives a child refuge at home. This ayah calls the Sacred House “مَثَابَةً لِّلنَّاسِ وَأَمْنًا,” a place people return to and find safety; it extends the home image to a shared sanctuary.

The section's dictionary form رَبُّ الدَّارِ means the owner of a house. This ayah calls God “رَبَّ هَٰذَا الْبَيْتِ,” the Lord of this House, directly joining the house image to its sustaining master.

The section joins shelter to the household's material needs. This ayah says the Lord of the House fed its people against hunger and secured them from fear (“أَطْعَمَهُم مِّن جُوعٍ وَآمَنَهُم مِّنْ خَوْفٍ”), completing the house's role as provider and refuge begun in 106:3.

The section's dictionary form رَبَّاهُ means “he raised him.” This ayah asks for mercy for parents “كَمَا رَبَّيَانِي صَغِيرًا,” because they raised the speaker when small; it makes childhood care and its return in mercy explicit.

The section defines upbringing as taking a child from one stage to the next. This ayah sets a complete two-year nursing period and assigns the father provision and clothing, spelling out the household labor and material support that sustain early growth.

The section describes gradual raising toward maturity. This ayah names a mother's carrying “وَهْنًا عَلَىٰ وَهْنٍ” and the child's weaning in two years, giving a bodily account of dependence and care as the child grows.

This ayah describes pregnancy, birth, and weaning before a person reaches maturity. It parallels the section's growth from dependence toward adulthood, while making the parent's labor behind that growth perceptible.

The section says a household includes those whose support one carries. This ayah calls wealth a means of support and directs people to provide food and clothing to those under their care, a specific parallel to the household provider's responsibility.

The section describes the household as including people whose livelihood is borne by another. This ayah ties a husband's household responsibility to his spending (“وَبِمَا أَنفَقُوا مِنْ أَمْوَالِهِم”), showing material provision as part of domestic care.

The section develops giving what a household member needs and receiving a vulnerable child into family life. This ayah names giving wealth, despite love of it, to relatives and orphans; it makes generous provision for the orphan a mark of righteousness.

When asked what to spend, this ayah names parents, relatives, orphans, the needy, and travelers as recipients. It connects the section's family-provider image to the concrete distribution of means to dependent people.

This ayah assigns a share of war gains to orphans, the needy, and travelers. The section's dependent household is one setting for provision; this verse extends provision to orphans through a public distribution.

This ayah directs that shared gains reach relatives, orphans, the needy, and travelers so wealth does not circulate only among the rich. It extends the section's household support for dependents into a community measure.

The section connects an orphan's vulnerability with those who support people in need. After 90:15 names the orphan near of kin, this ayah adds feeding “مِسْكِينًا ذَا مَتْرَبَةٍ,” the person in extreme want; it completes the passage's scene of feeding the vulnerable.

The section moves from receiving an orphan to its opposite, neglecting the vulnerable. This ayah condemns failure to encourage feeding the needy; beside 89:17's failure to honor the orphan, it shows that both dignity and material care are denied.

The section says the orphan must not be humiliated and describes the household as responsible for dependents. This ayah condemns devouring inheritance greedily; beside 89:17, it may evoke exploitation of an orphan's inheritance, though the verse itself does not specify whose inheritance.

The section places an orphan's dignity beside the provider's responsibility. This ayah condemns failure to urge feeding the needy; beside 107:2's shoving of the orphan, it shows rejection joined to withholding care.

This ayah names oppressed men, women, and children calling for rescue from a town of wrongdoers. It is a specific counter-scene to the section's vulnerable orphan and its command not to subdue him: children under power need someone to stand for them.

The section's dictionary form الغِنَى under root غ ن ي calls marriage a form of enrichment and a fortress for the unmarried. This ayah commands marriage for the unmarried and says that if they are poor God will enrich them (“إِن يَكُونُوا فُقَرَاءَ يُغْنِهِمُ اللَّهُ”), directly meeting that secondary sense.

The section describes marriage as a way the household grows and invokes its dictionary gloss of marriage as a fortress for the unmarried. This ayah describes spouses as a source of tranquility, affection, and mercy, making the household's sheltering function explicit.

The section treats a home as a family whose members return to one another. This prayer asks for spouses and descendants who are “قُرَّةَ أَعْيُنٍ,” a household that brings comfort to the eyes, giving the family relation a specific emotional form.

The section says marriage enlarges the household and that a child may work for the family and bring what it asks. In this ayah, Moses' work for a household leads to a marriage proposal with its daughter; it is a specific meeting of domestic service and marriage, though not a literal bride being led to her husband.

The section's dictionary form الغِنَى under root غ ن ي names marriage as one kind of enrichment. This ayah uses the same root in يُغْنِيكُم in a promise of material sufficiency after the fear of poverty (عَيْلَة); the financial sense marks a boundary from the section's marriage sense.

The section quotes root ق ه ر in تَقْهَرْ as humiliating or subduing an orphan. This ayah calls God “الْقَاهِرُ فَوْقَ عِبَادِهِ,” the subduer over His servants; the contrast distinguishes divine sovereignty from a person's abuse of someone dependent.

The section describes a child whose father has died and a separate adult who takes responsibility for raising him. This ayah says “وَمَا جَعَلَ أَدْعِيَاءَكُمْ أَبْنَاءَكُمْ,” setting a boundary between caring for a child and claiming that he is one's biological son.

This ayah says adopted children should be called by their fathers (“ادْعُوهُمْ لِآبَائِهِمْ”), completing 33:4's distinction. It clarifies that a household can care for a child while preserving his lineage.

The section describes a household whose members return to one another and a child taken in from aloneness. This ayah says people will come to God “فُرَادَىٰ” and have left behind what they were given; it contrasts family support with each person's final solitude, though فردًا here means individually rather than the section's narrower sense of a rare, unmatched single thing.

The section's dictionary sense of yatim includes a unique, rare pearl. This ayah compares the young attendants of Paradise to “لُؤْلُؤٌ مَّكْنُونٌ” (protected pearls), a specific but indirect echo of the section's pearl image; it does not describe an orphan.

The section's dictionary sense of yatim includes the image of a unique pearl. This ayah likens its companions to “اللُّؤْلُؤِ الْمَكْنُونِ” (protected pearls), a limited parallel in value and preciousness, without depicting a fatherless child.

The section's dictionary sense of yatim includes a rare pearl. This ayah compares the young attendants to “لُؤْلُؤًا مَّنثُورًا” (scattered pearls); it supplies a concrete pearl image, though its context is not orphanhood.

The section begins with a child whose father has died and discusses the support carried within a household. This ayah assigns inheritance shares to sons and daughters when a parent dies, giving the fatherless child's material situation a concrete legal counterpart, though it addresses inheritance rather than foster care.

The section's dictionary gloss for قَهَرَ is to abase or humiliate the orphan. This ayah says a kind word and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury, setting a clear boundary: provision for a vulnerable person must not become a means of harming or degrading them.

The section describes household members returning care to one another, including the grown child who serves the family. This ayah commands gentle speech and humility toward aging parents; 17:24 then grounds that return in their raising the speaker when small. This verse's own contribution is the concrete conduct owed to the parents.

The section's dictionary account of آل describes a household whose members return to one another. Joseph sends his shirt to his father and tells his brothers to bring the family; this ayah begins the reunion that arrives in 12:99 and is completed in 12:100.

The section describes separated kin returning to one another. This ayah has Jacob recognize Joseph's scent as the caravan departs, a specific moment of a father's recognition before reunion; the link is limited because this verse does not itself show a household receiving anyone.

The section describes a household with dependents and a person who provides for them. Abraham says he settled some of his descendants in a barren valley beside the Sacred House and asks God to provide fruits for its people, making the household's dependence on provision explicit.

The section's dictionary form الغِنَى under root غ ن ي includes marriage as a kind of enrichment. After 24:32 addresses marrying the unmarried, this ayah speaks of those who cannot find means to marry and tells them to remain chaste until God enriches them; it supplies the boundary case to the section's marriage-as-fortress image.

The section describes dependents whose support someone bears. This ayah says the righteous have a known right in their wealth; 70:25 identifies the asker and the deprived as those who receive it. This verse's own contribution is that support is an established claim on wealth.

The section links household provision to those in need. This ayah identifies the recipients of the known right named in 70:24 as the asker and the deprived, specifying whose need the wealth is meant to answer.

The section describes those who carry the living of others and the needy who can themselves support a household. This ayah says a recognized share of the righteous people's wealth belongs to the asker and the deprived, making the provider's responsibility toward the needy explicit.

The section develops a home as both refuge and a place where dependents receive provision. In the verse after 2:125's Sacred House as a place of return and security, Abraham asks for the city to be safe and for its people to receive fruits; this ayah adds sustenance to the sanctuary's protection.

The section describes a householder and the people whose needs he carries. This ayah commands the Prophet to enjoin prayer on his family and says God provides for him, connecting household responsibility to care that includes spiritual instruction as well as material support.

The section presents the home as a place where someone takes responsibility for others. This ayah directly commands believers to protect themselves and their families from the Fire, extending the household's caretaker role to their family's ultimate well-being.

The section defines عِيَال الرجل as the people whose support he carries. This ayah's parable depicts a person unable to act who is a burden on his master, a specific image of dependence and another's responsibility for a dependent; the context is a parable about worship, not a child or household.
